Let GGG be a group. A submonoid M≤GM\leq GM≤G induces a preorder on GGG via a≤b  ⟺  a−b∈Ma\leq b\iff a-b\in Ma≤b⟺a−b∈M. Consider the support supp⁡M≔M∩−M\operatorname{supp}M\coloneqq M\cap-MsuppM:=M∩−M. This is exactly the equivalence class of 000, so the quotient poset forms an ordered group G/supp⁡MG/\operatorname{supp}MG/suppM. This order is total if and only if M∪−M=GM\cup-M=GM∪−M=G. Conversely, the positive cone {g≥0}\{g\geq0\}{g≥0} of an ordered group is a submonoid with zero support.

The story repeats for convex cones and modules over an ordered ring, and (with one slight variation) for semirings and rings. The story for modules is partially formalised in Mathlib at docs#PointedCone, and the one for groups and rings at docs#GroupCone and docs#RingCone. I would like to refactor Mathlib to unify these definitions and results.

I can think of two main ways to design the formalisation in a uniform way:

  1. Have generic classes IsSalient s := ∀ x, x ∈ s → -x ∈ s → x = 0 and IsGenerating s := ∀ x, x ∈ s ∨ -x ∈ s on any SetLike type over a type with negation.
  2. Define classes IsSalient and IsGenerating on the type AddSubmonoid _, making use of dot notation for convex cones and subsemirings.

The advantage of (1) is that it makes automation (simp, aesop) easier. The advantage of (2) is that it makes typeclass search easier. I don't have a good reference point for designing predicates on generic substructures. Does anybody have thoughts on how to proceed?
When you say "generic classes", do you mean that IsSalient and IsGenerating would be predicates on sets?

Yaël Dillies said:

When you say "generic classes", do you mean that IsSalient and IsGenerating would be predicates on sets?

No, on SetLike types. Like how docs#HasMemOrNegMem ("IsGenerating") is formalised currently.

So this will be a definition scheme, right? in the sense that you get one predicate for each SetLike type. As you know, we are moving away from definition schemes when dealing with morphisms. Shouldn't we move away from them when dealing with subobjects too?
Yes, it would be. And yes docs#RingHom.ker was on my mind when I asked this.

The problem is that set membership on a SetLike type works differently than bundled function application. That is, x ∈ s does not elaborate to x ∈ s.toSet. This means that, if S : Semiring R, then S.IsSalient := ∀ x, x ∈ s.toAddSubmonoid → -x ∈ s.toAddSubmonoid → x = 0. This expression simplifies to what we want, but it is not defeq to what we want, which makes matching on hypotheses of the form x ∈ s difficult. On the other hand, f x for a FunLike type elaborates to f.toFun x via a coercion, avoiding this issue.

Artie Khovanov said:

which makes matching on hypotheses of the form x ∈ s difficult

But do you rewrite x ∈ s hypotheses often?
Yeah true. But you do sometimes want to partially apply eq_zero_of_mem_of_neg_mem, especially when using automation like aesop. I suppose I can just add an extra lemma for each structure I work with.
How many generalisable lemmas are we talking about? 10? 100? 1000?
To be fair the number of extra instances in the other approach is very low too
IMO that's way too low a number to justify the overhead cost

Alright so something like
docs#HasMemOrNegMem, docs#PositiveCone.IsGenerating -> (Add)Submonoid.IsGenerating
docs#AddGroupCone, docs#RingCone, docs#PositiveCone.IsSalient -> (Add)Submonoid.IsSalient
Tagging @Bjørn Solheim because I've seen him do work on the convex cone side. Does my refactor seem reasonable?

Thanks for the tag. I believe you have a good suggestion (focusing on the more fundamental sub-monoid structure). The following might be relevant: the total order inducing criteria you are proposing is stronger than the current IsGenerating for ConvexCones (https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Geometry/Convex/Cone/Basic.html#ConvexCone.IsGenerating). Therefore there might be some issues regarding which terminology to use. Maybe IsTotal can be considered? For IsSalient I think the notions coincide with the current library version (possibly modulo the inclusion of zero).

Note that the ConvexCone definition is over positive scalars and thus is separate and different from the submodule over nonnegative scalars definition for PointedCones. There are transport mechanisms but this could be relevant for what you are envisioning. Both IsGenerating and Salient are defined for convex cones (and then later transported to pointed cones).

Thanks for the info!
"Generating cone" is, I believe, the standard name for the thing I want. The exact predicate is in Mathlib as docs#ConvexCone.IsReproducing, and they're equivalent for pointed cones over a ring.
The fact positive cones aren't submonoids is a bit annoying - are non-pointed cones used much in Mathlib? I think I will just redefine the predicates for submonoids.

Oh wow the design for docs#ConvexCone, docs#ConvexCone, docs#PointedCone is really strange - it's a series of coercions, instead of structure classes or projections. @Yaël Dillies have you seen anything like this before?
What's PositiveCone?
(fixed)
What design did you expect?
Either ConvexConeClass or a .toConvexCone non-coercion projection
We don't really use PointedCones as subobjects, and ConvexCone is rather odd as it doesn't even really represent subobjects!

I don't really get why docs#ConvexCone exists tbh. I know it's the pen-and-paper definition, but it's just an axiomatisation of docs#PointedCone (ie a semimodule over the positive cone of a ring) without the 0 point.
The situation with docs#PointedCone and docs#ProperCone seems more reasonable to me, it's just the closed subgroup design.

Yeah OK: the only place in Mathlib where docs#ConvexCone is used to prove things not about itself is for the Riesz Extension Theorem.
image.png
This theorem is not affected by changing docs#ConvexCone to docs#PointedCone.

I am sure there were reasons for choosing the path of ConvexCone as it exists in mathlib (although I am not familiar with them). But I would agree that PointedCones is more in line with the notion of conic/conical span/hull. And, while terminology choices are always difficult and multifaceted, I think convex cone terminology based on convex cones with nonnegative scalars is more common than the positive scalars only version (although it is mentioned on Wikipedia).

I'm not necessarily saying we should make this refactor now - but I am pointing out that doing so would be very easy. In particular, the predicates on docs#ConvexCone.Blunt and docs#ConvexCone.Pointed do not appear to be used at all except to bundle docs#ConvexCone into docs#PointedCone.
Basically I'm saying that we shouldn't worry about duplicating work done by docs#ConvexCone for docs#PointedCone, because I don't think there's actually any work being done.

From the copyrights: looks like docs#ConvexCone was written in 2020 by Yury, and docs#PointedCone was contributed in 2023 by Apurva Nakade.
@Yury G. Kudryashov do you remember the considerations that went into choosing the "strictly positive" definition of positive cones in vector spaces rather than the "non negative" one?
I don't remember

I think I've added them because they were needed as a dependency for something. I don't mind if you redefine them (assuming that people who actually care about this part of Mathlib don't mind either).
OK thanks, I suspected so (they're apparently needed for integration)
@ooovi saw that you are working in this area - do you have thoughts on the definition of convex cone? ^^

The terminology PointedCone is also perceived rather negatively whenever I speak to mathematicians working in optimization/geometry. "pointed" is usually used for what mathlib calls "salient". When we move away from using ConvexCone, does the name become available for PointedCone? Together with Olivia (@ooovi ) we are currently working a lot on faces and duality theory for cones and PointedCone is the more important concept throughout.
In fact, we never used ConvexCone. There is one case where one could consider using it: the relative interior of a PointedCone is a ConvexCone.

Yeah I agree: rename docs#PointedCone to ConvexCone. Then IsPointed can be a name for "I don't contain any lines", which I want to be a predicate on AddMonoid as described upthread. I think IsPointed would be a good name for the predicate: we say "positive cone of an ordered group/ring" instead of "pointed monoid/semiring," but "cone" is already used in "convex cone" which is unfortunate for uniform naming.
Although from a quick search "pointed monoid" can mean what Mathlib calls "monoid with zero"... ugh

Related question: does the notion of "support" of a cone, defined as the union of lines it contains, come up in convex geometry or optimisation? The "support" of a subsemiring (defined as C∩−CC \cap -CC∩−C) comes up in real algebra / ordered ring theory. So, a submonoid / subsemiring / convex cone is proper iff it has zero "support".

In convex geometry this is called the lineality space of a cone. We just introduced it as PointedCone.lineal in our recent (not yet approved) PR https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/33664
OK thanks! I will make sure to use that.
If we are going to make this refactor, I would caution against moving files, in case we have to move them all back. But maybe it's fine since my story will take a while to implement.

I guess one more question: I understand that the common term for "contains no lines" is "pointed," with "salient" sometimes used (most notably on Wikipedia). What is the common term in convex geometry for "the set of pointwise differences generates the space," or equivalently "the convex cone is not contained in a proper subspace"? I've seen "generating" and "reproducing".

I usually use "full-dimensional", thought that might be too geometric for your generality. I heard people say "essential" or "spanning". But "generating" sounds not wrong for me either. I don't really like "reproducing".

"generating" sounds a bit generic to me
"spanning" could work imo

OK well I've added it to my project, it seems to work fine
Will PR eventually
pinging @Mario Carneiro as the original author of the group/ring cone files

This whole file looks completely different from when I worked on it. Originally, it was not meant to be used as such, it was just a temporary structure used to construct a partial order when you want to define "x is positive" or "x is nonnegative" rather than "x < y" or "x <= y"

I guess people tried to give it more of a standalone mathematical meaning but it was really supposed to be a *Core kind of class, that's why I didn't want any infrastructure around it other than docs#IsOrderedRing.mkOfCone and the other versions for ordered groups and so on
OK cool (yeah that was me rewriting). I guess I'm rewriting again to unbundle and unify everything.

New question: it's been suggested in review (#33942) that IsPointed and IsGenerating should be defs rather than classes. Having to pass around IsPointed and IsGenerating as explicit arguments makes using dot notation for polymorphism more annoying. @Yaël Dillies or anyone else do you have thoughts on this?
(tagging @Eric Wieser and @Johan Commelin from the PR)
Can you give a short example of what you mean by the dot notation being annoying?

Before:

AddSubmonoid.eq_zero_of_mem_of_neg_mem.{u} {G : Type u} [AddGroup G] (M : AddSubmonoid G)
  [M.IsPointed] {x : G} (hx₁ : x ∈ M) (hx₂ : -x ∈ M) : x = 0

Subsemiring.IsPointed.eq_zero_of_mem_of_neg_mem.{u} {R : Type u} [Ring R] (S : Subsemiring R)
  [S.toAddSubmonoid.IsPointed] {x : R} (hx₁ : x ∈ S) (hx₂ : -x ∈ S) : x = 0

And then we can say M.eq_zero_of_mem_of_neg_mem, S.eq_zero_of_mem_of_neg_mem, S.toAddSubmonoid.eq_zero_of_mem_of_neg_mem and the x ∈ ? hypotheses are all in the right type.

Now:

AddSubmonoid.IsPointed.eq_zero_of_mem_of_neg_mem.{u} {G : Type u} [AddGroup G] {M : AddSubmonoid G}
  (hM : M.IsPointed) {x : G} (hx₁ : x ∈ M) (hx₂ : -x ∈ M) : x = 0

Subsemiring.IsPointed.eq_zero_of_mem_of_neg_mem.{u} {R : Type u} [Ring R] {S : Subsemiring R}
  (hS : S.IsPointed) {x : R} (hx₁ : x ∈ S) (hx₂ : -x ∈ S) : x = 0

Then hS.eq_zero_of_mem_of_neg_mem has hypotheses x ∈ S.toAddSubmonoid etc, because the type of hS is still AddSubmonoid.IsPointed. We could change the namespace to just Subsemiring, but then we have to do S.eq_zero_of_mem_of_neg_mem hS.

Artie Khovanov said:

Yeah I agree: rename docs#PointedCone to ConvexCone. Then IsPointed can be a name for "I don't contain any lines", which I want to be a predicate on AddMonoid as described upthread. I think IsPointed would be a good name for the predicate: we say "positive cone of an ordered group/ring" instead of "pointed monoid/semiring," but "cone" is already used in "convex cone" which is unfortunate for uniform naming.

Has there been any progress towards renaming PointedCone to ConvexCone?

No - but I have now added docs#AddSubmonoid.IsPointed and docs#AddSubmonoid.IsSpanning, so (the current version of) docs#ConvexCone is ready to be deprecated in favour of docs#PointedCone. Note that the two uses of "pointed" here mean different things.

Thanks for the update! I came back to the question because in our code we needed to define salient (aka pointed) and flat for PointedCone, and we currently do so just in terms of their ConvexCone counterparts. Can you tell me again what would be the intended future way to do so? Define it in terms of AddSubmonoid.IsPointed (or not redefine it at all and just use the AddSubmonoid version)?

And can we also have a def for "closed under pointwise negation", or in cone terms, the cone is actually a submodule. I thought Flat would be the perfect name for this, but ConvexCone disagrees. If it goes away, the name Flat becomes available. Currently it just means "not salient", which feels like a waste.

I came back to the question because in our code we needed to define salient (aka pointed) and flat for PointedCone, and we currently do so just in terms of their ConvexCone counterparts. Can you tell me again what would be the intended future way to do so? Define it in terms of AddSubmonoid.IsPointed (or not redefine it at all and just use the AddSubmonoid version)?

AddSubmonoid.IsPointed (dot notation means C.IsPointed works)
Awesome

Martin Winter said:

And can we also have a def for "closed under pointwise negation", or in cone terms, the cone is actually a submodule. I thought Flat would be the perfect name for this, but ConvexCone disagrees. If it goes away, the name Flat becomes available. Currently it just means "not salient", which feels like a waste.

Yeah flat makes sense, I agree. You should make the definition for AddSubmonoid and relate it to the support being equal to the whole submonoid.

Finally, in #36605 I introduce PointedCone.linSpan for the linear span of a cone (aka the smallest submodule that contains it). It is the natural counterpart to lineal, and I wonder whether you plan to generalize this as well? Or at least think it makes sense to generalize. In the cone context it is equivalent to Submodule.span, and it is mostly convenient for naming and being concise.
That's just the submodule closure! You shouldn't make a new definition.

I know, but I think I have good arguments to do it.

  • conciser statements
  • shorter and easier to look up lemma names (looking up names that contain linSpan is much easier than looking up names with something like submodule_span, and I don't know whether this is even a good way to encode it in names)
  • meaningful abstraction

You could argue that lineal does not deserve a definition because it is just "C inf -C". But we clearly agree it deserves a definition. Likewise, linSpan is just "C sup -C". That it coincidentally agrees with Submodule.span should be seen as a theorem. But defining it in terms of Submodule.span is more convenient for using lemmas about span.

I mean - lineal would otherwise have no API, whereas linSpan does already have lots of API. What I would do is prove a theorem that in this case the span has this form C sup -C. That's how it's done everywhere else in the library!

The cone context seems to warrant some exceptions: we already have PointedCone.span R as short for Submodule.span R≥0. Here too the API already exists and it works just fine using it. We also already internally worked a lot with linSpan and can say from experience that likewise using existing API works just fine.

If PointedCone.span would have been called hull or so, maybe things would be different. But now we have two span-s, both are very important in the cone context, and telling them apart is a pain in statements and names. This is to a large part were we are coming from.
Why not rename it to hull then? This sounds reasonable
I agree with Artie that we don't want PointedCone.linSpan

I pondered this before. This change will be tedious, so lets think this through carefully. Here are some considerations:

  • The name hull hides the fact that span-lemmas apply to it (more so than linSpan does).
  • PointedCone.span is not the last time we have some sort of span operation. What about affine hulls, convex hulls, ...; should we aim for a uniform naming scheme throughout, calling everything span or everything hull, or what's the rule? Maybe use span in linear settings, hull in affine settings? Wasn't there even some talk of a span notation on typeclass level earlier in this thread? That would't work then.
  • Again, this is a big change, requiring a lot of renaming of lemmas as well. (much bigger than introducing linSpan)

If the only reason for this change is to not have linSpan, then I think it is not worth the trouble.

Yaël Dillies said:

I agree with Artie that we don't want PointedCone.span

Do you mean PointedCone.linSpan?

Thinking about it a bit more, perhaps this is a neat approach: use span for submodules, cones etc (linear setting); use hull for affine subspaces, polytopes etc (affine setting). This way there is no confusion between the setting and it is never hidden when span/hull lemmas apply.
Exactly. I feel like this reflects literature usage quite well too
Great :) But so renaming to PointedCone.hull is off the table and we are back at the problem of linSpan.
Ah sorry, I thought you were putting cones in the hull list. In the literature, I have seen "cone hull", but never "cone span"

For me, "span" is restricted to operations that yield a symmetric set. We accept the name docs#Submodule.span for the subsemimodule hull" out of pragmatism, but such pragmatism does not apply to cones l

This distinction makes sense as well!

And the fact that span lemmas need to be used on hull, but are then harder to discover and find, is not a significant concern to you?
Btw affine hull is a common term (I think of affine subspaces as symmetric in this context)
What do you think about using PointedCone.span as an alias of Submodule.span R (note, not R≥0)? Same name, just different namespace, so I can use dot notation.

Yaël Dillies said:

For me, "span" is restricted to operations that yield a symmetric set. We accept the name docs#Submodule.span for the subsemimodule hull" out of pragmatism, but such pragmatism does not apply to cones l

Counterpoint: one still says that vectors span a cone.

Can we think about what would be best from an implementation and usability point of view? We can draw the span/hull distinction between

  • symmetric vs non-symmetric, or
  • linear vs affine

From the point of hiding applicable API, the last one seems less dangerous.

Martin Winter said

the fact that span lemmas need to be used on hull, but are then harder to discover and find, is not a significant concern to you?

I would put a big warning to this effect in the docstring of PointedCone.span and hope it's enough

That wasn't too bad: #36953
The main work is likely hiding in our own repo :see_no_evil:

Note that I eventually want to unify all these closure operators into one declaration (generic over SetLike types whose forgetful map to sets preserves arbitrary intersections). Suggestions for how to deal with the fact that this operator is variously called "closure," "span," and now "hull" are very welcome!

This is what I worried about when I said

Wasn't there even some talk of a span notation on typeclass level earlier in this thread? That would't work then.

I was worries this will make more problems once we switch to hull. My feeling is that lean/mathlib has currently no good (or no standardized) way to deal with the intrinsic need of mathematics to use different notations/names for one concept in different parts of math.

Yes, and the result is lots and lots of API duplication
The problem is that abbrev isn't transparent enough. We'll have to make use of notation here I think.
In any case what we certainly don't want is redundant definitions with no API.

@Martin Winter
I went through and made a draft PR demonstrating what removing docs#ConvexCone would look like. It's less work than I thought! I'll proceed with many small PRs working from leaf to root. Once this work has been done, docs#PointedCone can be renamed to ConvexCone.

Note: I haven't yet done any deprecations or moved unused (in Mathlib) lemmas and documentation from docs#ConvexCone to docs#PointedCone. These need to be done as part of the refactor so we don't regress.

I'm coming quite late to this. Is the current plan to simply remove (and not just rename) the weaker notion of convex cones with strictly positive scalars ? I'm okay with a renaming, but a complete removal seems a bit unfortunate : for example, when you're working with root systems and their Weyl chambers, you might want to talk about open Weyl chambers being open convex cones (hence not containing zero).
Do you need that these are cones (in these sense of closed under positive scalar multiplication), or merely that they are open convex sets?
I would think both. To be fair I am not really working in this area, I am just noting that this refactor would seem to prevent applying any API to open convex cones.

For example a typical thing to do is to project them on the sphere to get a simplicial complex (abstractly, of course geometrically it gives you curved triangles). This is definitely using the cone structure (although there are millions way to view this operation)

Note also that the typical way to define Weyl chambers (again, in the most basic setting, I don't know how well this generalizes) involves removing some hyperplanes, then taking connected components to get the open Weyl chambers, and finally taking the closures to get the closed Weyl chambers. So somehow to prove that the closed chambers are a closed convex cone, you first prove that the open ones are an open convex cone.

I have had a similar situation: the relative interiors of PointedCones are naturally ConvexCones. Still, I don't know the answers to

  1. How niche is this concept?
  2. Do we really need it (or will open convex set do)?
  3. If yes, what would be the least pain way to inplement it?
  4. Does it need a lot of duplication of API, and is this worth it?

Do we have a comparable situation somewhere else in mathlib?
Is there existing API for "a submodule without 0"?
I don't think so. Excluding 0 makes sense when you also restrict to positive scalars, but not in general, no?
.....oh, true. It would snag at ((-1) • _)
as a side note i'd like to recommend Keimel and Roth 1992, *Ordered Cones and Approximation* as a generally useful source to mine

I think we should at the very least make the definition of "convex cones" be the one with zero.

I think keeping the other notion is fine, I'm not an expert so I will just take the applications as given.

But as a matter of technical design the version with zero is easier to prove things about because you can use all the existing facts about (semi)modules. And others have said that the usual meaning of "convex cone" is the version with a zero.

Anyway this raises questions:

  1. Assuming(?) that we want ConvexCone to refer to a convex cone with a zero - that is, a sub-semi-module over the positive cone of the ring - what do we want to call a convex cone possibly without a zero - that is, a set closed under strictly positive linear combinations?
  2. What API should the latter have?
I still think that we should use the version with a zero where possible in applications, because it has more API.

Alternatively, and more radically, perhaps there is some way to unite convex cones with semimodules in the algebraic hierarchy? I believe @Yaël Dillies has thought about this in the past. The issue is the lack of a zero element for the SMul.
